narrative:
The model predicts you have a 34% chance of failing your final year, which is high enough that the school requires you to take remedial courses to help you succeed.

The three factors that most strongly shaped this prediction were your lack of desire to pursue higher education, your clean record of zero past failures, and your long daily commute to school. Surprisingly, not wanting to continue studying after this year was the single biggest reason the model leaned toward failure. Because nearly every student who passed expressed strong ambition for higher education, your answer stood out as a clear warning sign that you may not be fully committed to finishing strong.

Your zero past failures actually worked in your favor and pushed the prediction toward passing. Most students who passed also had no previous failures, so this was a positive but not enough to outweigh other concerns. Similarly, your 30-to-60-minute travel time pulled the prediction slightly toward passing compared with students who live even farther away; however, it still counts as a longer commute than the majority of successful students who travel under 15 minutes.

To improve, you should seriously reflect on your goals. If you can reconnect with reasons to aim higher after this year, that shift in motivation alone could dramatically change your trajectory. Reducing travel time where possible, cutting back on going out, and addressing your high weekend alcohol consumption would also free up energy for studying. Taking the remedial courses seriously gives you a practical path to turn this prediction around. (248 words)
